subtitle: Master chorus, phaser, flanger, and tremolo to create movement and texture in your guitar sound

introduction.title: Understanding Modulation
introduction.text: Modulation effects work by continuously varying certain parameters of your guitar signal—whether that's pitch, amplitude, frequency, or phase. This creates movement, texture, and life in your sound, transforming static tones into dynamic, evolving textures that can enhance everything from subtle rhythm parts to otherworldly lead sounds.
introduction.quote: Modulation effects don't just change your sound—they make it breathe, pulse, and move through space, adding the organic quality that makes electronic effects feel musical and alive.

cards.title: Common LFO Wave Shapes
cards.description: Low Frequency Oscillator (LFO) is the engine behind most modulation effects. It generates a repeating wave that modulates various parameters of your signal.
items: Sine: Smooth, natural modulation
Triangle: Linear up/down movement
Square: Abrupt on/off switching
Sawtooth: Gradual rise, sudden drop

cards.title: Key Parameters
items: Rate/Speed: How fast the LFO cycles
Depth: How much the parameter changes
Phase: Starting point of the wave cycle
Sync: Tempo-locked or free-running

cards.title: How Chorus Works
cards.description: Chorus creates multiple "voices" by slightly delaying and pitch-modulating copies of your signal. The subtle pitch variations simulate the natural imperfections when multiple musicians play the same part.

cards.title: Musical Applications
items: Clean Rhythm: Adds richness without distortion
Arpeggios: Creates shimmering, harp-like textures
Ballad Leads: Smooth, singing sustain
12-String Simulation: Octave chorus for jangly sound
Pro Tip: Use subtle chorus (low rate, shallow depth) for natural thickening, or dramatic settings for '80s-style textures

cards.title: How Phaser Works
cards.description: Phaser splits your signal, delays one copy slightly, then mixes them back together. This creates moving notches in the frequency spectrum, producing the characteristic "swooshing" sound.

cards.title: Musical Applications
items: Funk Rhythm: Percussive, rhythmic sweeping
Psychedelic Leads: Swirling, hypnotic textures
Space Rock: Atmospheric, otherworldly sounds
Progressive Rock: Complex, evolving timbres
Stage Count: More stages = deeper notches and more dramatic effect. 4-stage is subtle, 12-stage is very pronounced

cards.title: How Flanger Works
cards.description: Similar to chorus but with shorter delays (0.5-10ms) and more feedback. The very short delay times create dramatic comb filtering effects, producing the characteristic "jet plane" swoosh.

cards.title: Musical Applications
items: Rock Solos: Dramatic sweeps and buildups
Ambient Textures: Slow, evolving soundscapes
Sound Effects: Jet planes, whooshes
Filter Sweeps: Manual control for expressive sweeps
High Feedback Warning: Extreme feedback settings can create oscillation and very loud sounds. Start conservatively!

cards.title: How Tremolo Works
cards.description: Tremolo modulates the amplitude (volume) of your signal, creating rhythmic pulsing. It's one of the oldest effects, built into many vintage amplifiers.

cards.title: Musical Applications
items: Surf Rock: Fast, aggressive tremolo
Country: Subtle rhythmic pulsing
Ambient: Slow, breathing textures
Rhythmic Patterns: Synced to song tempo
Tremolo vs. Vibrato: Tremolo modulates volume, vibrato modulates pitch. Many guitar amps labeled "vibrato" actually produce tremolo!

fields.label: Expression Pedal Control
fields.value: Control rate or depth with an expression pedal for real-time modulation shaping.

fields.label: Tempo Sync
fields.value: Lock LFO rates to song tempo for rhythmically relevant modulation (1/4 notes, 1/8 notes, etc.).

fields.label: Manual Mode
fields.value: Turn off the LFO and manually control the sweep for precise, musical phrasing.

fields.label: Chorus + Delay
fields.value: Classic combination for lush, spacious lead sounds.

fields.label: Phaser + Distortion
fields.value: Place phaser after distortion for dramatic, harmonically rich sweeps.

fields.label: Tremolo + Reverb
fields.value: Pulsing ambient textures, great for atmospheric parts.

cards.title: What to Avoid
items: Using the same rate for all modulation effects
Maximum depth settings that overwhelm the dry signal
Ignoring the musical context and tempo
Combining too many modulation effects simultaneously
Using effects as a crutch for poor playing technique

cards.title: Best Practices
items: Start with subtle settings and gradually increase
Match modulation rates to musical phrases
Use tempo sync when appropriate
Consider the other instruments in the arrangement
Learn to play cleanly before adding modulation

cards.title: Phase Relationships
cards.description: When using multiple modulation effects, consider how their LFOs interact
items: In-phase: Effects reinforce each other
Out-of-phase: Creates complex, evolving patterns
Different rates: Creates beating and interference patterns

cards.title: Stereo Modulation
cards.description: Stereo modulation effects can create width and movement
items: Opposite phase LFOs for ping-pong effects
Different rates on left/right for complexity
Stereo chorus for wide, enveloping textures

exercises.title: Exercise 1: LFO Rate Relationships
items: Set up a chorus effect and play a sustained chord
Very slow (0.1-0.5 Hz): Subtle, almost imperceptible movement
Slow (0.5-2 Hz): Natural, musical breathing
Medium (2-5 Hz): Obvious but musical
Fast (5-10 Hz): Dramatic, effect-heavy
Notice how each rate creates a different emotional impact and musical character

exercises.title: Exercise 2: Effect Comparison
items: Play the same musical phrase (try an Am pentatonic run) through each modulation effect
Chorus: Notice the thickening and shimmer
Phaser: Hear the frequency notches sweeping
Flanger: Feel the dramatic jet-plane swooshes
Tremolo: Experience the rhythmic pulsing
This helps you understand when each effect is most musically appropriate

exercises.title: Exercise 3: Tempo-Synced Modulation
items: Use a metronome at 120 BPM and practice these tempo relationships
Tremolo at quarter note rate (2 Hz at 120 BPM)
Phaser at half note rate (1 Hz at 120 BPM)
Chorus at whole note rate (0.5 Hz at 120 BPM)
Learn to hear how modulation can enhance or fight against the song's rhythm
